newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Short Australia debt off amid growing rate jitters.
newsitem.headline: Short Australia debt off amid growing rate jitters.

text.p: *The short end of the Australian bond yield curve came under pressure on Wednesday following a strong Tankan report and as concerns grew over next week's RBA board meeting.
The short end of the Australian bond yield curve came under pressure on Wednesday following a strong Japanese Tankan report and as concerns grew over next week's Reserve Bank board meeting.

A 50 basis point rate cut in current official interest rates had been largely priced in since the weak labour force report earlier this month, and while analysts still believe the board will endorse such a move, some doubts are now creeping in.
A sell recommendation of three-year bonds by an influential U.S. investment bank added to the bearish tone, which filtered through to bill futures contracts.

Rory Robertson, interest rate strategist at Bankers Trust Australia, said he had been bullish on 10-year bonds from around 7.50 percent to 7.00 percent and on three year bonds from 6.50 percent to 5.75 percent.

But, "Now that those targets have been achieved, we're neutral -- not bearish. But if it pulls back we're buyers," Robertson said, adding that he still gave a 75 percent chance of an easing although the timing remained the unknown factor.
The Reserve Bank board meets on July 1, but adding to the uncertainty over local policy will be the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on July 1 and 2.
Futures rallied at the opening on a more stable U.S. market, but were knocked back after the Tankan survey showed the key diffusion index at plus seven when a small fall had been seen.

Analysts said the data would probably bring forward expectations of a tightening in Japanese monetary policy, and although there would still be a vast policy gap to Australia, it would narrow yield differentials between the two.

Japanese interest rates currently stand at 0.5 percent against domestic official 5.5 percent rates. But if the RBA did ease Japanese investors could switch their sights on higher yielders such as the U.K., New Zealand, and the U.S., they said.
Before today's sell-off some traders had been discussing the benefit of holding some short positions going into next week on a risk/reward basis given that an easing had been priced in.

They pointed to the possiblity of the Reserve holding policy unchanged combined with the threat of the May retail trade data on July 2 coming in stronger than expected. Retail trade recorded its first back to falls for three years in March/April, suggesting a statistical rebound in May.
Meanwhile, the focus switches to the U.S. where May durable goods orders and a US$15.0 billion five year note auction are due later on Wednesday.

Short-end spreads to the dollar bloc widened sharply by the close against the bloc, while long dated stocks were mixed. The yield curve also flatten sharply. The market was once again outpaced by New Zealand debt ahead of Thursday's N.Z. budget and despite some profit-taking there.
